blocks.text: VI. Junius, thinking he could avoid these Symplegades by a new interpretation, rendered this passage as follows: There arose a great famine in Samaria, etc. so that the fourth part, the belly itself, which is in the hollow of doves, was of five shekels of silver. But at first reading it is immediately apparent that this exceedingly learned man would not have rendered it thus, almost, I would say, without any sense, had he not felt himself to be in great straits. For what would the fourth part, the belly itself of doves be? And what point was there in specifying that the belly is in the hollow? Although the hollow is rather in the belly than the belly in the hollow. [col. 42] Again, how could it have entered the mind of that man, who was most perspicacious, that the belly of doves was sold separately? Nor can what is found in his version, the fourth part, the belly itself, which is in the hollow of doves, be extracted by any torture from the Hebrew words רובע הקב חריונים. For if רבע, the fourth part, and הקב, the belly, as the distinguished Junius renders it, were in apposition, each noun would have the He hajedia, or article, prefixed, as one would say in Greek τὸ τέταρτον, ἡ κοιλία [to tetarton, hē koilia]. I add that in this version קב kab is wrongly confused with קבה keba. Of these, קבה keba means belly or crop; but קב kab is something quite different, namely κάβος [kabos], cabus, a kind of measure. So it is explained among the Hebrews by the Aruch, Kimchi, Pomarius, Elias and Aquinas in their Lexicons, by Mardochaeus in his Concordance, by Alphes in the tractate On Passover, ch. 5, fol. 176, and by the Gloss on the Talmud passim. Hence the compound תרקב tharkab means to some two cabs, as if contracted from תרי קבין there kabin, two cabs; to others, more correctly, three cabs, as if it were תרי וקב, two and a cab, one more. So R. Selomo in various places of the Talmud. And κάβος [kabos] is also a measure in Hesychius, Philoxenus, the Suda, the Etymologicum, Phavorinus and others. Finally, none of the ancients renders חריונים otherwise than as dove's dung. Let Josephus and the Greek, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Latin translators be consulted, and, among the Hebrews, Iarchius, Kimchi and R. Levi on this passage. Among them a remarkable agreement will be found, which rarely happens in the interpretation of an obscure passage. Indeed, of the more recent writers no one dissents except Junius and Fuller, about whom now a few words.
